$comment: Shared test vectors for the sharded summary store. Asserted by BOTH suites:
indexer/crates/cli/tests/summary_vectors.rs and mcp/test/summaryShards.test.ts.
The point is that the Rust indexer (sole writer) and the TypeScript MCP
server (reader) resolve a merged shard to the SAME winner. If they disagree,
the server serves prose the next index is about to overwrite. Both sides read
these exact lines and must agree line for line, so a change to either
implementation that drifts from the other fails here first.
There are TWO resolution rules and both are pinned here:
dedupe     — records found WITHIN one source, resolved by content alone
supersedes — folding a whole newer-provenance source onto an older one
They differ on an equal summary_at, deliberately. See each section's `rule`.
shard_keys are Rust-only: they exist so the committed layout cannot change
silently, but TypeScript never computes a shard key — it enumerates shard
files with readdir, which is why no BLAKE3 implementation is needed there.

shard_key.algorithm: first 2 lowercase hex chars of BLAKE3(node_id utf-8)

rule: Records claiming the same id are reduced to one winner:
1. greater summary_at wins (missing summary_at counts as the empty string)
2. tie -> the byte-lexicographically smaller RAW SOURCE LINE wins
Byte order over the raw line (never a re-serialization) is what lets two
languages agree without sharing a serializer.
Identical duplicate lines collapse silently and are NOT conflicts.
Every non-winning DIVERGENT record is preserved as a conflict, never dropped.
Lines starting with a git conflict marker are skipped with a warning.

cases.name: single record passes through
union merge duplicated an unchanged line
newer summary_at wins regardless of file order
newer summary_at wins with the file order reversed
equal timestamps fall back to raw-line byte order
a record with no summary_at loses to one that has it
unresolved merge markers are skipped and both sides survive
diff3 markers are skipped too
malformed and id-less lines are dropped, valid ones are not

$comment: These lines hold LITERAL UTF-8 characters, not \u escape text, and
that is the point: the tiebreak compares the bytes of the line as it
sits in the shard. Writing the characters as escaped \\u sequences
would leave the escape TEXT in the line, so the comparison would run
over ASCII 'u','d','f' and pass for entirely the wrong reason. If you
need an escape here, use a single backslash so it resolves when the
fixture itself is parsed — never a doubled one.
cases.name: unicode prose round-trips and compares by utf-8 bytes

$comment: The case that motivated comparing encoded bytes rather than a
language's native string `<`. U+FFFD encodes as EF BF BD; U+10000 as
F0 90 80 80, but in UTF-16 it is the surrogate pair D800 DC00.
UTF-8 byte order puts U+FFFD first (EF < F0); JavaScript's `<`, which
compares UTF-16 code units, puts the astral character first
(D800 < FFFD). The two orders DISAGREE, so this vector fails on any
implementation that reaches for the native comparison — which is
exactly the drift it exists to catch.
cases.name: utf-8 byte order breaks the tie, not utf-16 code-unit order

$comment: A summary field that is PRESENT but says nothing is not a summary.
Rust once tested this with contains_key and TypeScript with
typeof === 'string', so a null-valued line was a record on one side
and malformed on the other. With a late summary_at it then WON the
tiebreak in Rust and evicted real prose into conflicts.jsonl, while
the server went on serving the prose. Both sides now require a
NON-EMPTY STRING, and this vector is what holds them to it.
cases.name: null, non-string and empty summaries are rejected, not ranked
a purpose_summary alone is enough, but only as non-empty prose

$comment: Cross-source folds — the OTHER resolution rule, and the one where a
silent loss actually happened: an unconditional last-source-wins insert
let a stale local sidecar overwrite a teammate's newer committed summary
with nothing recorded anywhere.
Each case folds `older_source` first, then `newer_source` on top, the way
the indexer folds legacy harvest -> committed shards -> database -> this
machine's sidecars. Lines within one source resolve by `beats` (see the
dedupe section); the fold BETWEEN them uses the rule below.
rule: A record from the newer source displaces the incumbent unless it is
STRICTLY OLDER by summary_at:  candidate.summary_at >= incumbent.summary_at.
This deliberately differs from `beats` on an equal summary_at, and the
difference is load-bearing. summary_at is DAY-PRECISION (PRD §6.2.5 keeps
wall-clock time out of committed bytes), so an agent re-summarising a node
that was already summarised today produces a tie. Breaking that tie by
byte order — what `beats` does — would discard the rewrite: the agent's
work would silently not take. Provenance settles what the data cannot.
Determinism is unaffected: the same shards plus the same sidecars resolve
identically on any machine. Provenance is an input, not a clock.
Byte-identical records dedupe silently and are never conflicts.
Every displaced record is preserved, under either rule.

cases.name: a newer source with a newer summary_at displaces, and the loser is recorded

$comment: THE REGRESSION. A teammate's summary arrives in a committed shard; this
machine still holds a months-old sidecar for the same node. Folding the
sidecar last must NOT overwrite the newer record, and the record that
loses must still be written down.
cases.name: a newer source that is strictly older by summary_at does not displace

$comment: An equal summary_at goes to the NEWER SOURCE, not to byte order. The
prose is chosen so the two rules visibly disagree: 'aaa old' sorts
first, so `beats` would keep it and drop the rewrite. Same-day
re-summarisation is the common case, not a corner one.
cases.name: an equal summary_at goes to the newer source, not to byte order

$comment: The boundary, stated as a test: the SAME two records, same day, both in
ONE source. There is no provenance to appeal to, so byte order decides
and 'aaa old' wins — the opposite outcome to the case above. If an
implementation ever collapses the two rules into one, exactly one of
these two cases fails.
cases.name: the same tie inside one source still goes to byte order

$comment: A line with an id and a late timestamp but no prose is not a summary.
Admitting it would let it WIN on summary_at and evict real authored
text — a record with nothing in it must never displace one.
cases.name: an id-only line in the newer source cannot evict authored prose

$comment: The same rejection, for a field that is present but empty of prose.
This is the shape the reviewer reproduced live: a null-valued summary
with a late timestamp, arriving from the newer source, evicting real
prose into conflicts.jsonl on the Rust side while the TypeScript
reader skipped it — so the server and the indexer disagreed about
what the node's summary was.
cases.name: a null-valued summary in the newer source cannot evict authored prose

$comment: A re-index sees its own output in the shards and the same record in a
sidecar it has not consumed yet. Reporting that as divergence would
train people to ignore conflicts.jsonl.
cases.name: a byte-identical record from both sources is not a conflict
records for different ids from both sources all survive
